catalog_quote: Hyman 1977:38 (local scanned copy): "Many stress languages however are described as having at least some words lacking a stress, e.g. Kitsai (Bucca and Lesser 1969:13), Saho (Welmers 1952:147) and Seneca (Chafe 1960:21). While it is often pointed out that certain 'clitics', i.e. forms which attach themselves to other forms (which in turn take a stress), do not have an inherent stress, stresslessness seems to be of greater significance in the above languages." | StressTyp2 lect 617 Kitsai, primary pattern 'StressTyp2 code IRR (IRR)'; passage 1193: "Some words lack stress. (Hyman 1977:38)"; passage 1194 (StressTyp2 editors on the primary): "(Buca & Lesser find IRR unsatisfactory in their paper but they do not offer a better analysis)."

audit.recode_to: Keep 'lexical (irregular, non-strict)' for now; if Bucca & Lesser 1969:12-13 describe stress as freely varying/'unstable' rather than word-contrastive, reclassify as undetermined / no fixed stress (not demonstrably lexical).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: the Hyman 1977:38 sentence is verbatim in the held scanned excerpt and the two StressTyp2 passages match the local StressTyp2 dump. (2) But the deciding evidence is entirely second-hand: Hyman's one sentence (about stressless words, not placement), StressTyp2's IRR code with the editors' note that Bucca & Lesser themselves found IRR unsatisfactory, a 2010 Survey snippet and a Ruhlen database field. The primary (Bucca & Lesser 1969, 13 pp.) is unread. (3) Vantine 1980, downloaded now from U Manitoba MSpace and verified on page images, adds the closest thing to a primary reading we have: Bucca 1969:12-13 treats stress and pitch as 'unstable' and their distinctiveness as 'indeterminate'; stress is marked inconsistently in Lesser's texts; Vantine states no rule and omits suprasegmentals.
